summary: West Pointer, Army pilot and Pershing's 'chief air scout' in 1916, who set a 250-mph speed record in 1923 and commanded France Field, Panama; John's 2nd-great-grand-uncle.
bio:
Leo Gerald Heffernan was born on 23 April 1889. He graduated from West Point in 1911 and was commissioned in the 5th Cavalry, serving at Fort Myer, Virginia, in 1913 and 1915. In May 1916 he earned pilot certificate no. 489 and flew with the 1st Aero Squadron on the Mexican border and in Mexico during the Punitive Expedition. His father's obituary called him 'chief air scout to General Pershing', and his own described him as Pershing's aviation aide and pilot and 'one of the first American fliers to come under enemy gunfire'. He married Mathilde Payne in Chicago on 24 December 1915; their daughter Regina died in 1920.

In 1917, as a captain in the 3d Aero Squadron, he went to the Aviation School at San Antonio, his wife joining him there, and from November 1917 to January 1918 he commanded Wilbur Wright Field in Ohio, where a Bain News Service photograph of 1917 shows him with three other officers. He also commanded Kelly Field and led the 12th Aero Squadron. From September 1918 to May 1919, with the American Expeditionary Forces in France, he was Air Service commander of the IX Army Corps and in turn commanded the 2d Army Observation Group, the 4th and 5th Pursuit Groups and the 2d Day Bombardment Group.

After the war he commanded the 3rd (Attack) Group at Kelly Field in 1922 and then the flying group at Fort Bliss under the 1st Cavalry Division. In February 1921 he directed the air search for Lt. Alexander Pearson, lost over the Big Bend, and in December 1922 he led five planes of the 12th Observation Squadron from Fort Bliss to join the search for Col. Francis Marshall. On 24 March 1923 the War Department announced 'the fastest flight on record': 250 miles an hour over the 75 miles from Columbus, New Mexico, to Fort Bliss at El Paso, covered in eighteen minutes in a DH-4B 'in a blinding sandstorm' with a 100-mph wind behind him, on a trip that had begun at Nogales. The record was unofficial, but Time magazine reported it and the Journal of Education ran the story as 'Outspeeding the Birds'. In April 1925 he published 'Co-operation Between Cavalry and Air Service' in The Cavalry Journal.

From 1928 to 1930 he was assistant commandant and then commandant of the Air Corps Technical School at Chanute Field, Rantoul, and from 1930 to 1932 he commanded France Field in the Panama Canal Zone. His obituary says that 'such promising young flyers as Jimmy Doolittle and Claire Chennault' served under him, a family-supplied claim that is probably true. He was treated at Walter Reed in 1933 and retired that September as a major. From 1934 to 1949 he was the Anheuser-Busch representative in central California. His second wife was Jane Hamilton Davis (1902–1975), born at Pleasant Hill, Louisiana, and later buried at Arlington; their daughter Elizabeth Jane was born in 1922. He died of a heart attack in Los Angeles in February 1956, on the 7th or the 9th according to differing notices, and was buried at Wilkes-Barre after a funeral there on 15 February 1956.
notable: Set a 250-mph speed record on 24 Mar 1923; commanded France Field, Panama; Doolittle and Chennault served under him (obituary)

researchNotes:
Leo Gerald Heffernan was born 23 Apr 1889. He graduated from West Point in 1911 and joined the 5th Cavalry; at Fort Myer in 1915. He earned FAI pilot certificate #489 in May 1916 and flew with the 1st Aero Squadron on the border and in Mexico during the Punitive Expedition; his father's obituary calls him 'chief air scout to General Pershing' and his own obituary 'General of the Armies John J. Pershing's aviation aide and pilot' and 'one of the first American fliers to come under enemy gunfire'. In May-Jun 1917, as Capt., 3d Aero Squadron, he went to the Aviation School at San Antonio (his wife joined him). In 1917-18 he commanded Wilbur Wright Field (Nov 1917 - Jan 1918) and Kelly Field and led the 12th Aero Squadron. Sep 1918 - May 1919 in the AEF he was Air Service commander, IX Army Corps, and in turn commanded the 2d Army Observation Group, 4th and 5th Pursuit Groups and 2d Day Bombardment Group. 1922-25 he commanded the 3rd (Attack) Group at Kelly Field (1922), then the Fort Bliss flying group under the 1st Cavalry Division. On 24 Mar 1923 the War Department announced 'the fastest flight on record': 250 mph over 75 miles from Columbus, NM, to Fort Bliss in a DH-4B 'in a blinding sandstorm' with a following wind; Time covered it (31 Mar 1923) and the Journal of Education ran it as 'Outspeeding the Birds'. In Apr 1925 he published 'Co-operation Between Cavalry and Air Service' in The Cavalry Journal. 1928-30 assistant commandant then commandant of the Air Corps Technical School, Chanute Field; 1930-32 commander of France Field, Panama Canal Zone. Treated at Walter Reed in 1933 and retired as Major. 1934-49 Anheuser-Busch representative in central California. His obituary says he commanded 'such promising young flyers as Jimmy Doolittle and Claire Chennault' (family-supplied; probable). He married (1) Mathilde Payne in Chicago in 1915 (daughter Regina d. 1920) and (2) Jane H. Davis (daughter Elizabeth Jane, b. 1922). He died of a heart attack in Los Angeles/Hollywood in Feb 1956 - 7 Feb per the 18 Feb notice, 9 Feb per the 25 Feb notice and Dwyer - with funeral and burial at Wilkes-Barre on 15 Feb 1956. A 1917 portrait is credited to the Library of Congress.

Library of Congress Bain News Service glass negative LC-B2-4268-9 shows "Capt. L. G. Heffernan" with three other officers at Wilbur Wright Field, Ohio, in 1917, when he commanded the field ([R4-S7]); it carries no known restrictions and was downloaded. Contemporary newspapers on Chronicling America add two rescue missions: in Feb 1921, as commander of aviation at Fort Bliss, he directed the air search for Lt. Alexander Pearson, lost over the Big Bend ([R4-S1]), and in Dec 1922 he led five planes of the 12th Observation Squadron from Fort Bliss to join the search for Col. Francis Marshall ([R4-S2]). The San Antonio Light of 24 Mar 1923 gives detail of his record flight: 75 miles from Columbus, N.M., to El Paso in 18 minutes in a sandstorm, with a 100-mph upper wind behind him, on a trip that began at Nogales; the record was "not official" ([R4-S3]). The Evening Star noted his transfer from Rantoul to the Canal Zone in Sept 1930 ([R4-S4]), and the Washington Times listed him as retired in Sept 1933 ([R4-S5]). FamilySearch adds that he married Mathilde Payne in Chicago on 24 Dec 1915, and that his second wife Jane Hamilton Davis (1902-1975) was born at Pleasant Hill, Louisiana, and is buried at Arlington; his death (9 Feb 1956, Los Angeles) is backed by a California county death record ([R4-S8]).
